summary: Defines a MIB module of textual conventions for commonly used pseudowire management information. Other pseudowire MIB modules can import them rather than each defining its own versions.

plainLanguage.summary:
A pseudowire is an emulated connection carried across a packet network, and the routers that carry it expose information about it for monitoring. That information is published in a MIB, a table of named values that a management program can read over SNMP.

This document defines the vocabulary for those values: the names for identifiers and indexes, the list of operational states a pseudowire can be in, the fault bits, the control word states and the fragmentation states. Other management modules can import these names instead of defining their own.

questions: what is a textual convention in a mib
subtitle: A shared set of SNMP textual conventions so pseudowire management modules describe the same values the same way.

tldr.problem: Each SNMP management module for pseudowires tends to invent its own way of expressing the same things: how a pseudowire is identified, whether it is forwarding, whether its control word was negotiated, and whether fragmentation is in use. Management systems then have to understand several dialects.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module, PW-TC-STD-MIB, that holds textual conventions only. A textual convention names a value and says how it is to be displayed and what it may contain, so that other modules can import it and use it for their own objects.
tldr.outcome: Other pseudowire management modules can import the same conventions instead of defining their own. The module defines no management objects of its own, so it has no direct effect on the security of the Internet, and it is registered at { mib-2 188 }.

today: RFC 5542 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the PW-TC-STD-MIB module, registered at { mib-2 188 }, for import by other pseudowire management modules.

sections.title: Why a Shared Set of Conventions
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it defines textual conventions used for pseudowire (PW) technology and for Pseudowire Edge-to-Edge Emulation (PWE3) MIB modules.

A textual convention is not a managed object and does not hold a value that a manager reads. It is a named type: it says what a value means, how it should be displayed, and what values it is allowed to take. The MIB module defined here, named PW-TC-STD-MIB, contains only such conventions, and its intent is that they will be imported and used in pseudowire-related MIB modules that would otherwise define their own representations.
sections.plainLanguage: Several teams write management modules for pseudowires, and each tends to describe the same idea in its own way. This document gives them one shared vocabulary, so a value called an operational status means the same thing everywhere.

sections.title: The Management Framework This Builds On
sections.content:
For a detailed overview of the documents that describe the current Internet-Standard Management Framework, the RFC points the reader to section 7 of RFC 3410.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base or MIB. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol. Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the Structure of Management Information. This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to SMIv2, which is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580, all of which are STD 58.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a named list of values on a device. A manager reads it over SNMP. The names and the shapes of those values follow a common notation, and this document uses that notation to define its conventions.

sections.title: Identifiers, Indexes and Groups
sections.content:
The module is identified as pwTcStdMIB, is rooted at { mib-2 188 }, and carries a single revision dated 21 April 2009, described as the original version. Each convention has a display hint of d, meaning that the value is shown as a decimal number, and a status of current.

PwGroupID is an administrative identification for grouping a set of service-specific pseudowire services, with syntax Unsigned32. PwIDType is the pseudowire identifier, used to identify the pseudowire, together with some other fields, in the signaling session; it too has syntax Unsigned32.

PwIndexType is the pseudowire index: a unique value, greater than zero, for each locally defined pseudowire, used for indexing several MIB tables associated with that pseudowire. It is recommended that values are assigned contiguously starting from 1, and the value for each pseudowire MUST remain constant at least from one re-initialization to the next re-initialization. Its syntax is Unsigned32 (1..4294967295).

PwIndexOrZeroType extends that convention by permitting the additional value of zero. The zero value is object-specific and MUST therefore be defined as part of the description of any object that uses this syntax; examples of its use include situations where the pseudowire was unknown, or where none or all pseudowires need to be referenced. Its syntax is Unsigned32 (0..4294967295).

PwAttachmentIdentifierType is an octet string used in the generalized Forward Error Correction element for identifying attachment forwarders and groups. A NULL identifier is of zero length, and the syntax is OCTET STRING (SIZE (0..255)). PwGenIdType represents the Attachment Group Identifier type and the Attachment Individual Identifier type in generalized FEC signaling and configuration, with syntax Unsigned32 (0..254).

PwCfgIndexOrzero is an index in any of the relevant configuration tables for supplementary information regarding the configuration of the specific technology. The value zero implies that no additional configuration information is applicable, and the syntax is Unsigned32 (0..4294967295).
sections.plainLanguage: These conventions name the values that identify a pseudowire and the rows that hold its information. A pseudowire gets a number of its own that stays the same across restarts, and a second number that indexes the tables where its details are kept.

sections.title: Status, Control Word and Fragmentation Values
sections.content:
PwOperStatusTC indicates the operational status of the pseudowire. It has six values. up(1) means ready to pass packets. down(2) means the pseudowire signaling is not yet finished, or indications available at the service level indicate that the pseudowire is not passing packets. testing(3) means the administrative status at the pseudowire level is set to test. dormant(4) means the pseudowire is not in a condition to pass packets but is in a pending state, waiting for some external event. notPresent(5) means some component is missing to accomplish the setup of the pseudowire, which can be a configuration error, incomplete configuration, or a missing hardware component. lowerLayerDown(6) means one or more of the lower-layer interfaces responsible for running the underlying packet switched network is not in the up state.

PwStatus indicates the status of the pseudowire and the interfaces affecting it, as a set of bits: pwNotForwarding(0), servicePwRxFault(1), servicePwTxFault(2), psnPwRxFault(3) and psnPwTxFault(4). If none of the bits are set, it indicates that no faults are reported.

PwCwStatusTC indicates the status of the control word negotiation, based on the local configuration and the indications received from the peer node. waitingForNextMsg(1) means the node is waiting for another label mapping from the peer. sentWrongBitErrorCode(2) means the local node has notified the peer about a mismatch in the C-bit. rxWithdrawWithWrongBitErrorCode(3) means a withdraw message has been received with the wrong C-bit error code. illegalReceivedBit(4) means a C-bit configuration with the peer that is not compatible with the pseudowire type. cwPresent(5) means the control word is present for this pseudowire: if signaling is used, the C-bit is set and agreed upon between the nodes, and for a manually configured pseudowire the local configuration requires the use of the control word. cwNotPresent(6) means the opposite. notYetKnown(7) means a label mapping has not yet been received from the peer.

PwFragSize gives the desired fragmentation length in bytes; if set to zero, fragmentation is not desired for packets bound for the packet switched network. PwFragStatus indicates the status of the fragmentation and reassembly process, based on local configuration and peer capability, as a set of bits: noFrag(0), meaning the local configuration is for no fragmentation; cfgFragGreaterThanPsnMtu(1), meaning the local node is set to fragment but the fragmentation size is greater than the MTU available between the nodes, so fragmentation is not done in that case; cfgFragButRemoteIncapable(2), meaning the local configuration conveys the desire for fragmentation but the peer is not capable of reassembly; remoteFragCapable(3), meaning the remote node is capable of accepting fragmented protocol data units; and fragEnabled(4), meaning that fragmentation will be used on this pseudowire, which requires that the local node was configured for fragmentation, that the peer can accept fragmented packets, and that the control word is in use.
sections.plainLanguage:
These conventions say what state a pseudowire is in. There is a list of six operational states, from up through down and testing to dormant and not present, and a set of fault bits for the cases where something is wrong with forwarding or with the packet network underneath.

Two more sets of values cover the optional features. The control word states say whether the two ends agreed on the control word, and the fragmentation bits say whether packets are being split to fit a smaller link.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This module does not define any management objects. Instead, it defines a set of textual conventions that may be used by other PWE3 MIB modules to define management objects.

Meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define management objects. The RFC therefore states that this document has no impact on the security of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The module defines no values that can be read or set, so it adds nothing that could be attacked. The security questions belong to the modules that use these conventions to publish real objects.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The MIB module in this document uses the IANA-assigned OBJECT IDENTIFIER value recorded in the SMI Numbers registry. The descriptor pwTcStdMIB is assigned the value { mib-2 188 }.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is registered under a fixed number so that other modules can point at it and import from it.

items.label: down
items.desc: Signaling is not yet finished, or service-level indications say the pseudowire is not passing packets.

items.label: testing
items.desc: AdminStatus at the pseudowire level is set to test.

items.label: dormant
items.desc: Not in a condition to pass packets, but waiting for some external event.

items.label: notPresent
items.desc: Some component is missing to accomplish the setup of the pseudowire.

items.label: lowerLayerDown
items.desc: One or more lower-layer interfaces running the underlying packet switched network is not up.

items.label: waitingForNextMsg
items.desc: Waiting for another label mapping from the peer.

items.label: sentWrongBitErrorCode
items.desc: The local node has told the peer about a mismatch in the C-bit.

items.label: rxWithdrawWithWrongBitErrorCode
items.desc: A withdraw message was received with the wrong C-bit error code.

items.label: illegalReceivedBit
items.desc: A C-bit configuration with the peer that is not compatible with the pseudowire type.

items.label: cwPresent
items.desc: The control word is present for this pseudowire.

items.label: cwNotPresent
items.desc: The control word is not present for this pseudowire.

items.label: notYetKnown
items.desc: A label mapping has not yet been received from the peer.

items.title: Identifiers
items.text: PwGroupID groups services, PwIDType identifies a pseudowire in the signaling session.

items.title: Indexes
items.text: PwIndexType numbers each locally defined pseudowire; PwIndexOrZeroType allows zero as well.

items.title: Configuration index
items.text: PwCfgIndexOrzero points at a row in a technology-specific configuration table.

items.title: FEC identifiers
items.text: PwAttachmentIdentifierType and PwGenIdType name attachment forwarders and groups.

items.title: Operational status
items.text: PwOperStatusTC gives six states, from up to lowerLayerDown.

items.title: Faults
items.text: PwStatus carries five bits covering forwarding and receive or transmit faults.

items.title: Control word
items.text: PwCwStatusTC reports the outcome of control word negotiation with the peer.

items.title: Fragmentation
items.text: PwFragSize and PwFragStatus describe the desired and actual fragmentation state.
